# F7 · Account, access and session

*Extracted verbatim from the PRD, which remains the single source of truth for every criterion below. Edit the PRD, then regenerate — never edit this file.*

Identifiers in this file: `F7-AC-01` – `F7-UP-05`.

#### F7 · Account, access and session

| Section | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Priority | **Must.** 2.2's second objective states getting this wrong has an unbounded cash cost — never optional, at any point in the build. |
| Serves | The second objective in Section 2.2 — private by construction, cheap to run — and the Section 2.5 constraint that says the same thing: nobody but the manager can reach the app or cause it to spend, since each run costs real money. |
| Design note | There is no invite code. An invite code is a bearer credential — whoever holds it can create an account, and it can be forwarded to someone the owner never chose. For a set of users that is known, tiny and enumerable (one person, possibly two more later), the correct mechanism is not to hand out secrets but to remove self-registration entirely: **nobody can create an account; accounts are created by the owner.** That is less to build, tighter, and revocable in one action. |
| Happy path | The manager enters his email address, receives a six-digit code, types it in, and is in. His session then carries him for weeks without logging in again. On first use he links his FPL team once by team identifier, and that first open behaves exactly like the start of a new gameweek. |
| **Acceptance Criteria** |  |
| **F7-AC-01** | **There is no sign-up.** Public registration is switched off at the authentication provider; an account exists only because the owner created it. |
| **F7-AC-02** | A stranger with the URL cannot register, cannot cause a code to be sent, and cannot learn from the response whether one was sent or whether any given address has access. Submitting the form cannot itself be prevented — preventing it would reveal which addresses exist — so the requirement is that nothing follows from a submission on an unauthorised address. |
| **F7-AC-03** | **No passwords anywhere.** Authentication is a one-time six-digit code emailed to an authorised address, short-lived and single-use. |
| **F7-AC-04** | A typed code is used rather than a tappable link, deliberately: on a phone, a link opened from a mail client lands the session in that client's embedded browser rather than the one the manager is using. |
| **F7-AC-05** | The login screen gives the same response whether or not the address is authorised, so it cannot be used to enumerate who has access. |
| **F7-AC-06** | **Code requests are rate limited, and the limit is invisible:** at most one code per address per sixty seconds, with a small hourly ceiling per address and a matching ceiling per source address. |
| **F7-AC-07** | A throttled request returns exactly the response an accepted one returns, so the screen cannot be used to discover the limit any more than to discover who has access. Without this the email field is an open send button: a stranger still cannot get in, but can flood an authorised inbox and burn the provider's send allowance. |
| **F7-AC-08** | The **Send another code** control carries a visible cooldown once used. |
| **F7-AC-09** | **A code dies after five wrong attempts** and a fresh one must be requested. Six digits inside a ten-minute window is brute-forceable if attempts are unbounded; the attempt limit, not the code length, is what makes the code safe. |
| **F7-AC-10** | **The session is long and sliding** — thirty days, renewed on each visit. For weekly use that means signing in about once, which is what makes a passwordless flow tolerable rather than irritating. |
| **F7-AC-11** | **Per-user data isolation is enforced by the database, not by application discipline.** Every table carrying user data has a row-level security policy keyed to the signed-in user from the first migration onward, while there is still only one user. A forgotten filter in application code must not be able to expose another account's squad, calls or stored judgement. |
| **F7-AC-12** | **Spend is capped at the API provider, not by an in-app counter** — see the Cost control NFR, which owns this requirement in full. |
| **F7-AC-13** | The FPL team is linked once, by team identifier, on a dedicated first-run screen. No FPL account credentials are ever requested, transmitted or stored, and the app never writes to FPL. |
| **F7-AC-14** | **The identifier is confirmed before it is linked.** The entered ID is resolved against the public FPL API and the team it returns — team name, manager name, overall rank — is shown back for the manager to accept or reject before anything is stored. A mistyped identifier is usually still a valid one belonging to a stranger; without confirmation it would link silently and every call afterwards would be built on someone else's squad with nothing on screen to say so. |
| **F7-AC-15** | Onboarding is one screen and one run: the team link on first log in, then the first advice run, which behaves exactly like the start of a new gameweek. Beyond that link screen there is no tour, no settings pass and no second onboarding state. |
| **F7-AC-16** | **The Landing screen is the only screen reachable without an account, and the only one without the app header.** One card, two tabs: *What he does* (default) — five one-line claims, each expanding to a sentence and driving a small device mock beside it; sales rather than function, no feature list, no pricing, no scroll — and *Log in*. |
| **F7-AC-17** | Invite-only is stated up front on the Landing screen, as a badge under the wordmark, so a visitor learns before typing anything that an unrecognised address gets them nowhere. |
| **F7-AC-18** | The Landing screen carries no sign-up path, no password field and no "forgotten your password?" line. |
| **F7-AC-19** | A standing disclaimer sits at the foot of the Landing screen: not affiliated with the Premier League or Fantasy Premier League, advice only, the manager makes his own moves in the FPL app. |
| **F7-AC-20** | Errors on the Landing screen are stated inline in a red card inside the login card, never as a transient toast. |
| **F7-AC-21** | **The account sheet is reached from the avatar in the header on every screen that carries one.** It is headed by the portrait, the team name and the manager identifier with the current gameweek, and holds the manager's identity and the only route out of the session. |
| **F7-AC-22** | Nothing is listed in the account sheet before it works — no disabled "coming later" rows. Rare and destructive actions live here rather than in the Squad screen's thumb-reachable strip. |
| **F7-AC-23** | The account sheet belongs to the screen it was opened from, and cancelling returns there untouched. |
| **F7-AC-24** | The session can be ended from the account sheet, with confirmation on a second page of the same sheet rather than a stacked overlay, stating that the squad and the week's decisions are kept and what is needed to return. |
| **F7-AC-25** | Confirming log out leaves the session and returns to the Landing screen on its Log in tab. There is no per-screen signed-out view. |
| **F7-AC-26** | Settings are deliberately absent until they do something. |
| **Unhappy Paths** |  |
| **F7-UP-01** | **An unrecognised address is entered.** Acceptance: no email is sent, no account is created, and the screen says exactly what it says for a recognised address. Nothing distinguishes the two. |
| **F7-UP-02** | **A code is wrong, expired or already used.** Acceptance: the error is stated inline in a red card within the login card, never as a transient toast, and a fresh code can be requested. After five failures the code is spent, and the inline error says so rather than leaving the manager retyping a code that can no longer work. |
| **F7-UP-03** | **Codes are requested repeatedly.** Acceptance: after the first, further requests inside the window send nothing while returning the same screen and the same words. Neither a stranger nor the manager can tell a throttled request from an accepted one; the manager simply finds **Send another code** on cooldown. |
| **F7-UP-04** | **A stranger reaches the URL.** Acceptance: nothing about any squad is shown before sign-in, and there is no route to create an account. |
| **F7-UP-05** | **A second person is given access.** Acceptance: the owner creates their account directly at the provider; no code is issued, nothing is shared, and removing them is deleting the account and ending their session. Their data is isolated by the row-level policies already in place. Spend is not isolated: the prepaid provider balance is a single shared cap, and a second person draws on the same £50 — which is accepted at this size, but is the reason a second account is a decision rather than a formality. |
